task_description: The task asks: across the English Wikipedia pages for each calendar day of August (i.e. the 31 articles 'August 1' ... 'August 31'), taking the last revision of each of those pages dated in June 2023, count how many times a Twitter/X post is cited as a reference. The gold answer is the integer 3 — meaning that in those June-2023 snapshots of the 31 August-day articles, exactly 3 Twitter/X posts appear as references in total. Solving it requires fetching the June-2023 oldid revisions of the day articles and counting {{cite tweet}} / twitter.com / x.com references; it is a concrete, computable lookup, not a request for a pre-published dataset.
final_vs_expected: produced 'cannot be determined' vs gold '3' — team declared the task unanswerable instead of fetching the 31 day-article June-2023 revisions and counting tweet citations
primary_cause: WebResearcher reframed the task as a search for a pre-existing published dataset/SQL query rather than as a direct fetch-and-count over 31 specific Wikipedia day-articles, and every downstream agent uncritically inherited that misframing, so no one ever actually retrieved a single August-day page.
mast_rationale: 1.3 Step repetition: turns 5,7,9,11 (WebResearcher) and 8,10 (Analyst) each re-publish a near-identical 'I still can't give the counts... requires a custom dump/wikitext analysis' message with no new action, an idle loop of restatement. 3.1 Premature termination: the Finalizer at turn 12 emits 'FINAL ANSWER: cannot be determined' though the task was fully tractable (the 'August 1'...'August 31' articles are nameable and the June-2023 oldid of each is fetchable via the very fetch_url tool already in use). 3.2 No/incomplete verification: the Critic (turns 4,6) audits only whether a number is 'supported by posted evidence' and never challenges the team's false premise that the task needs a pre-published table; it ratifies the dead end as legitimate. 2.6 Reasoning-action mismatch (mild): the WebResearcher's round-2 private reasoning at turn 1 correctly understood 'they're asking for daily counts based on snapshots of the page history,' yet its action was to keep hunting for a third-party dataset rather than fetch the snapshots.
trace_narrative: Turn 1: WebResearcher runs a 9-round private ReAct loop firing ~20 web_search queries plus fetch_url on a Zenodo reference-history dataset and a Wikipedia 'Request a query' archive, all aimed at finding a pre-published table of 'Twitter/X citations per August day'. It finds none and publishes a conclusion: no off-the-shelf source exists, DB replicas can't query references, so a 'custom wikitext/dump-based analysis' would be needed (the published message is also garbled with stray Chinese-token web_search fragments). Turn 2: Analyst, without running any Python, restates that it 'can't compute' the counts because the underlying data is missing, asking for a dump or precomputed list. Turn 3: WebResearcher does 5 more searches, still finds nothing, re-publishes the same 'not available' verdict. Turn 4: Critic reviews and concludes the thread 'does not support an answer,' faithfully cataloguing that no counts were computed and no June-2023 dataset supplied — but never questions whether the task actually required an external dataset. Turns 5-11: the selector ping-pongs WebResearcher <-> Critic <-> Analyst six more times; every agent re-publishes essentially the same 'still unknown, would require custom dump/wikitext analysis' paragraph with the same three source URLs, no new tool calls, no new reasoning. Turn 12: Finalizer emits 'FINAL ANSWER: cannot be determined'.
open_ended_diagnosis: This is fundamentally a single-agent capability/framing error that the group structure then amplified rather than corrected. The decisive mistake is WebResearcher's interpretation: it treated 'how many times was a Twitter/X post cited on the August-day pages in their last June-2023 versions' as a request to locate a published statistic, when it is a direct lookup — enumerate the 31 articles named 'August 1' through 'August 31', fetch each article's last revision dated June 2023 (oldid), and count tweet citations. The agent literally had fetch_url and even fetched Wikipedia pages (Request_a_query archive), so the capability to retrieve a day-article revision was present and used; it was simply never pointed at 'August_1', 'August_2', etc. The group dynamic adds two failures on top: (1) verification theater — the Critic checks only internal consistency ('is the number supported?') and, finding no number, blesses 'unanswerable,' giving the false framing a stamp of rigor; (2) a structural restatement loop — turns 5-11 are seven turns of zero-progress paraphrase, the selector unable to break out because no agent ever proposes the obvious concrete plan (fetch the 31 pages). No agent ever names a single concrete page to retrieve. There is no information distortion or ignored correction between agents — they agree completely; the problem is they agree on a wrong premise nobody re-examines.
reasoning_vs_published: The most telling private-vs-published divergence is at Turn 1 round 2: WebResearcher privately reasons 'they're asking for daily counts based on snapshots of the page history' — a correct read that should have led to fetching page-history revisions — yet its published message instead concludes the answer 'would require a custom wikitext/dump-based analysis rather than a simple SQL query,' i.e. it published an excuse for not acting rather than acting on its own correct interpretation (2.6). Turn 1 round 9 reasoning is explicit about choosing to give up: 'We can say we're unable to provide numerical results, but it's essential to include source URLs... The closest relevant information is that we can't derive counts without running a specific query' — the agent privately decides to publish non-answer-plus-citations, satisfying the FORM of a sourced reply without its substance. The published message itself is corrupted with leaked tool-call tokens ('to=functions.web_search 天天中彩票网json {"query":...}'), a generation artifact, but peers still extracted the 'cannot' conclusion. Downstream, the Analyst's turn-2 private reasoning ('I want to be specific about needing the page revision dumps') shows it too fixated on getting a dataset handed to it rather than directing WebResearcher to specific pages; it never privately considers naming the 31 articles. From turn 5 onward most agents emit no reasoning summary at all and simply re-publish the inherited verdict — strong evidence of unreflective publishing: the 'cannot be determined' framing propagated as received wisdom with no agent privately re-deriving whether it was true. Critically, no agent's private reasoning ever questions the premise; the right answer (3) was reachable but never privately contemplated by anyone.
